Absolutely. Here’s the **call brief I’d want in front of me if I were walking into the second call having never met Steve**.

## Steve B. — Second Call Brief

### Who Steve is and what he is building

Steve is opening a **new wellness and recovery center in Ocean City, Maryland**, likely within the next **3–4 weeks**, depending on equipment delivery. They are **pre-revenue and not yet open**, so this is not a traditional “fix what’s broken” prospect. The opportunity is to help him **build the right growth system before opening**, rather than undoing bad systems later. fileciteturn0file0

The business will offer:

- Cryo slimming
- Cryofacials
- Red light therapy
- Wellness pod services
- Body composition scans
- Peptides, including Retatrutide and BPC-157, with more planned
- Supplements and weight-loss products

The overall experience is meant to feel more like a **high-end wellness and recovery spa** than a traditional medical practice. Most services are noninvasive and designed around relaxation and feeling good.

### His biggest priority: memberships

This is the most important thing to remember going into the call.

Steve explicitly said:

> “I’d rather have a hundred members than have to keep chasing more new clients every day and week.”

**That is his pain point and desired outcome.**

He does not want to build a business that constantly depends on finding another one-time customer. He wants **predictable recurring revenue through memberships**.

So I would frame the conversation around:

**“Steve, what stood out to me from your first conversation was that you don’t want to open this business and immediately put yourself on the hamster wheel of constantly chasing the next new customer. You want to build a strong membership base. That is actually why I wanted to personally talk with you.”**

### Where he is right now

Steve is still building almost everything:

- Pricing is not finalized.
- Packages are not finalized.
- Memberships are not finalized.
- Hours are not finalized.
- Marketing has barely started.
- His website is being built.
- A friend is doing some basic “coming soon” Facebook content.
- He has not launched a real acquisition strategy.
- He is setting up Boulevard for payments, collections, and business operations.
- He is talking to at least one other company, so **there is competition for this deal**.

This is actually your strongest positioning opportunity. He does **not** just need someone to “run ads.” He needs someone to help make sure the business is commercially structured correctly **before the doors open**.

## The core issue you should diagnose

His stated issue is **memberships**, but the deeper issue is:

**He has a collection of services, equipment and products, but he does not yet have a complete customer acquisition and lifetime-value strategy connecting them together.**

The questions you need to answer on this second call are:

1. **Who is his ideal recurring member?**
2. **What service gets someone through the door initially?**
3. **What should the membership actually include?**
4. **How does someone naturally move from a first visit into a membership?**
5. **How do peptides, weight loss, body composition, cryo, red light and recovery services cross-sell into each other?**
6. **How will leads be followed up with and booked?**
7. **How will the team be trained to sell the membership without making the experience feel pushy?**
8. **What happens after someone becomes a client to increase retention, referrals and lifetime value?**

That is where TLC can be much more valuable than a company simply selling him leads.

## The angle I would take with him

Do **not** approach this as:

> “We can build you a membership.”

That makes TLC sound like a membership consultant and reduces the size of the problem you solve.

Instead:

**“The membership is one piece of the entire system. We need to make sure the right people are coming through the door, that the introductory offer naturally leads into the membership, that your team knows how to convert them, and that the experience keeps them coming back. Otherwise, you can have the best membership in Ocean City and nobody buys it.”**

Then explain that your advantage is that you can help him build the **entire growth ecosystem from day one**:

**Market diagnosis → offer strategy → lead acquisition → follow-up and booking → conversion → membership → retention → referrals.**

That is the end-to-end story.

## What I would say at the beginning of the call

Since you have never met him, acknowledge it naturally without making the handoff feel awkward:

> “Steve, it’s great to finally meet you. I reviewed the conversation you had with my team, so I’m familiar with what you’re building and where you are in the process. The biggest thing that jumped out at me was what you said about wanting 100 members instead of constantly chasing new customers. I completely agree with that goal. But I also want to make sure we build the entire system around that goal, because a membership by itself doesn’t create recurring revenue. The way you attract people, what brings them in initially, how your team converts them and what happens after that first visit all have to work together.”

Then get him talking:

> **“Before I show you what I think we should do, tell me more about what you envision when you say you want 100 members. What would you ideally want those members coming in for every month?”**

That question will tell you whether he has actually thought through the economics or whether “100 members” is simply an idea.

## The biggest opportunity I see

His service mix is potentially **very membership-friendly** because he has repeat-use wellness services rather than one-and-done procedures.

You could potentially build a customer journey such as:

**Entry offer → body composition baseline → personalized wellness/recovery plan → recurring membership → peptide/weight-loss upsell → supplements → referrals**

But I would **not prescribe the exact membership before understanding his pricing, margins, equipment capacity and local market**.

That gives you a perfect reason to sell the diagnostic component of TLC:

> “Before we tell you what membership to launch or what ads to run, we need to understand your market, your competitors, what people in your area are already buying, how they’re pricing it and where the opportunity actually is. Otherwise, we’re guessing with your money.”

## Important questions you still need to ask

The first call left several major gaps. I would focus your discovery on these areas:

- Who exactly are the four decision-makers, and **who has final authority**?
- What is the total investment already made in the business?
- What monthly revenue does he need to break even?
- What is his desired revenue at 6 and 12 months?
- What is his planned marketing budget?
- What are the proposed membership prices?
- How many appointments can the facility realistically handle per day?
- What is the margin on each core service?
- What services does he expect to be the main acquisition offers?
- Who will answer and follow up with new leads?
- Who will sell memberships?
- What does “100 members” mean financially? $99/month? $299/month? $500/month?
- Is his target market primarily year-round locals, seasonal residents, tourists, or some combination?
- How seasonal is the Ocean City market, and what is the strategy for slower months?
- What is the role of the peptide business, especially since he was already selling peptides before the location opened?
- What are the other partners expecting from a marketing/growth partner?

### One thing I would be careful about

The first call told him that **“we’re not a marketing agency”** and emphasized that TLC focuses primarily on what happens after the lead comes in. That is not fully aligned with your current positioning as an **end-to-end agency**.

I would gently reset that on this call without contradicting your team:

> **“You may have heard my team talk a lot about what happens after the lead comes in because that is one of the biggest things that separates us from a typical marketing agency. But to clarify, we absolutely handle acquisition as well. We just don’t believe our job ends when we hand you a lead. We look at the entire journey.”**

That is important because he is actively talking to other companies, and you do **not** want him thinking he needs to hire one company for marketing and TLC separately for memberships and retention.

## Your main objective for the call

You are not selling him **“help with memberships.”**

You are selling him the opportunity to **launch correctly from day one** instead of spending the next year piecing together five different vendors, changing offers, wasting ad spend, retraining staff and fixing systems after they fail.

The central message should be:

> **“Steve, you have a unique advantage right now because nothing is broken yet. We have the opportunity to build this correctly before you start spending heavily to acquire customers. Our goal would be to make sure the market strategy, offers, acquisition, follow-up, membership conversion and retention systems are all designed to work together from the beginning.”**

### The one sentence to remember before the call

**Steve does not want more random customers. He wants a predictable base of recurring members, and your job is to show him that getting to 100 members requires an entire end-to-end growth system, not just creating a membership package.**
